be used to determine the distance between those two cities. 986

Secondly, the instance of *376 i, zi at its lower side is not used as a form of the demonstrative, as attested
for the beginning of the text, but as an integral part of the ending of the form expressed by the column in
question. If we leave out the number with which this column ends for a moment, it reads in sum SARA-
sa4-i and the ending of which the polyphone *376 forms an integral part can be positively identified as
that of the D pl. in -ai (see WOUDHUIZEN 2011: 131-132).

Working along this line of reasoning, the noun SARA-sa4- can be explained as an adjectival
derivative in -s(a)- of the nominal root sara- which in variant writing sa5+r?- is attested for § 27 of the
Emirgazi text where it definitely expresses the meaning “smoke offering” (WOUDHUIZEN 2004: 62).

It may safely be concluded, therefore, that by means of the sequence of signs in the second
column of line 2 reference is made to subsidiary offerings made at the inauguration ceremony of the stele
Çalabverdi 3, expressed in the dativus sociativus. With the authors of its editio princeps, finally, I am
inclined, on the bases of consultation of the photographs presented by them, to identify the number at the
lower right side of the column as “3” rather than “2”.

In sum, this leads us to the following transliteration and interpretation of the text on stele
Çalapverdi 3 in its entirety:

1.

“This stele, prince Anazitis has placed

TUWA 3 á-na-ZITI-i

on that trade. It did so in various ways: by concluding treaties with rulers in whose
territories at least 37 Assyrian types of commercial organization (kārum ‘colony’ and
wabartum ‘trading post’) were established; by empowering these settlements; by giving
the eponym of Assur (līmum) and his oice, the City Hall, a role in crucial aspects of
trade; by expanding the legal framework to act upon trade-speciic situations; and by
creating a system of long-term joint-stock investments called naruqqum.
Old Assyrian (OA) society centred around the concepts of honour and dignity, a
shame society. Violation of the accepted norms would bring shame on the transgressor
and could ultimately lead to his isolation from society. In this respect, OA society does
not difer from the rest of Mesopotamian civilization.2 The socially acceptable Assyrian
merchant was an awīlum ‘gentleman’, the opposite of which was a lā awīlum. Apart
from being reliable and trustworthy, the main quality of a ‘gentleman’ was the ability
and willingness to grant favours (gamālum) and help people in need. This was not
unique to OA society.3
A typical example of a favour is contained in the letter TTC 18: “This is what Išme-
Aššur said, speak to Imdilum: Before you left you asked from me a textile. In front of
Šu-Hubur you said: ‘Give me a kutānum and as soon as I arrive (in Kanesh) I will send
you the equivalent out of my own money, and I will do you a favour.’ You have not
sent me the equivalent out of your own money. If you are my brother, do me a favour!
I am a man of favour(s), I will do you a favour (in return). Send me my tadmiqtum with
the very irst envoy! I bought a house. (It will be) as if you made me a present.”4 Išme-
Aššur had given a textile to Imdilum in Assur for which the latter would send an
appropriate amount of money in payment. This type of sale was called a tadmiqtum.
Despite Imdilum having made his promise before a respected merchant, he had not
yet sent the money. However, the sender of the reminder letter remains keen on
maintaining a good relationship with Imdilum, and he stresses his ability to grant a
favour. His motivation appears from line 24. Although it will be his own money, he
assures Imdilum that he will be as glad as if he had given it to him as a present. In
general, the (future) beneiciaries take great care to stress their gratitude.5 The favours
to be done in Assur primarily consisted of buying merchandise before money sent
from Kanesh had arrived, which amounts to granting an interest-free loan. According

2. THE MERCHANTS
There was a social distinction in Assur as well as in the Assyrian communities abroad
between ‘big’ (rabium) and ‘small’ (ṣahhurum) free citizens (awīlum). It was deined
along family lines, as a remark by the daughter and sons of the deceased Pūšu-kēn
makes clear when they write in BIN 6, 59: “And since (Kulumāya) left he has shown
contempt towards our father’s spirit and [even] us he has thereby [treated] as ‘small’
persons”.17 Attaining a good position could be the responsibility of an adoptive father.18
Families and individuals from both layers of society were actively involved in trade,
with the merchants belonging to the ‘big’ people, the citizens holding slaves. Others
besides professional merchants bought and sold to make some extra money. In the
irst place there were the female relatives of the traders, who manufactured textiles
at home and sold these via their men in Anatolia. The king of Assur also entrusted
merchandise to a trusted merchant, but it is not known how often the kings did this.

Occasionally there appear to have been temporary shortages of silver, but this did
not afect buying. It is known that copper was widely used as a means of payment in
Assur, but there is as yet little evidence for its use in the export trade. Five textiles
were bought with copper in KTB 2:8. Only one instance is known where a caravan is
largely paid for with copper. According to KTS 2, 36 + Bursa 3776, 100 kutānus, 20 bags,
the harness of the donkeys and the payment for the sa’adum were all paid with copper
(worth 10 minas 18 1/2 shekels of silver at 100:1), whereas the 4 donkeys, the 20 minas
of hand-tin and the exit-tax were paid in silver (2 minas 47 2/3 shekels). The whole
caravan was eventually paid with the silver that had been sent to Assur. Apparently,
the representatives in Assur had preferred to use copper until the silver arrived from
Kanesh.
In Anatolia, there will have been a continuous demand for tin and high quality
textiles, partly due to the re-exporting of these commodities to more distant places,
such as Purušhattum, and Assur was the sole intermediary delivering tin to Anatolia.
With a more or less steady demand, there are two main factors that account for price
luctuations: the availability of money, usually in the form of silver and copper, and
the level of supply of imported goods. Moreover, the longer the term for commission
sales, the higher would be the expected returns.50 If silver was in short supply, cash
sales were impossible. One had to wait until better times and exploit possible
alternatives. According to KTS 1, 18: “Do you not hear that silver is hard to obtain and
that there is no payment for textiles? Silver is hard to obtain here. You say in your
tablet: ‘Sell my merchandise at any price and come here!’ There is gold as payment,
let us obtain gold for you. We will stay for one or two months and then obtain silver
for you. Since you did not order it, we did not want to take gold.”51 Some shortages
were known to last for a limited time only, such as those caused by harvesting or a
festival.52

Gold has a special position among the objects of trade.77 It was a highly prized material
and one letter contains the somewhat deprecatory remark “When they see gold, (their)
hands and feet tremble” referring to unspeciied “men” (awīlū).78 It was made into
jewellery and formed the valuta of the naruqqum-joint-stock investments in a way that

10.3 The attorney (rābiṣum)
To solve complex legal cases, one could hire an attorney. According to the Erišum
inscription found in Kültepe, the attorney was made available by the palace in Assur.
Texts from everyday life show that the right to engage an attorney was granted by an
oicial decision made by the city council. A suitable person could then be selected
and instructed and an agreement reached about his wages (igrū) and how they would
be paid together with his expenses (gamrum, ukultum, dātum). Usually the attorney
received half of his wages in Assur and the rest after completing his task. Attorney’s
wages are known to range from 30 (Iddin-Aššur, Kt c/k 128), to 50 (Laliya, TC 1, 24),
or even 55 shekels of silver (Aššur-ṭāb, TC 1, 24). The danger that a hireling would
suddenly give up his mission also applied to attorneys. Their contract contained the
stipulation that in such a case they would have to repay the money already received.128

Šu-Ištar was married in Kanesh to a woman by the name of Watniašwe, who is called
his maid (amtum) in Kt c/k 18, but elsewhere his wife (aššutum).6 Despite her Anatolian name,

7.2.4 Datum and 'communal pouring' at other colonies
Most of the available documention regarding sitapkum, the depositing of wares
on accounts, and the payment of the datum-contribution concerns the state of affairs
at the Kanish colony. This is caused by two factors: most of the evidence has been
discovered at the site of ancient Kanish, and that colony held a pre-eminent position
in the OA colonial system. Kanish was, however, not the only Assyrian institution in
Anatolia to charge datum and hold a settlement of accounts.

Sumi-abia, KEL 113/IV, they will add 135 grains per mina as monthly interest.
Mannum-ki-Assur, Sn-Istar and Ili-nâdâ received the silver on behalf of the colony. 334
The text of these debt-notes has in fact been copied, because the original debt-notes were
among Enlil-bâni's tablets that were sent to Assur.
Two debt-notes explicitly mention the receipt of silver by three eponyms acting for
the colony, CCT 1, 4 [C] and that recorded in TC 3, 213. This demonstrates that these
loans were made in kind and did not result from a sale or other financial obligation, such
as that mentioned in CCT I, 4 [A]. While it apparently took three representatives of the
colony to contract a loan on its behalf, two kin-um-eponyms were present when the
obligation described in CCT 1, 4 [A] arose.
Compared with Enlil-bâni's other financial claims, the rate of interest of 135 grains
per mina per month, equalling 15 per cent annually, is very moderate in view of the
standard rate of interest among Assyrians fixed by the Kanish colony at 30 per cent per
year.
A rate of 15 per cent is not confined to dealings with the colony because it also occurs
as the rate of default interest in a debt of La-qép son of Sö-Assur to Enlil-bâni in CCT I,
2: 57. Twice this rate, 1 1/2 shekels per mina per month, occurs in TC 3, 213: 7, 25 //
CCT I, 2: 28; CCT 1, 2: 41, 47, 53; and Pa. 4: 34 (no default), 47 (no default), 53 (no
default), 57.
On the other hand, 20 per cent (I shekel per mina per month) occurs in CCT l, 2: 6,
17, 35 (no default); Pa. 4: 5 (no default), 18 (no default), 23 (no default), 29 (no default),
and 40 (no default). It is clear that Enlil-bâni charges a special low rate of interest in his
dealings with specific debtors, among whom was the Kanish colony. It is not known what
the colony offered in return for this favourable treatment. The colony itself paid 20 per
cent on the amounts it received as withdrawal fees (see 11.8).
Assur-malik, the father of Enlil-bâni, is the creditor in two of the debts recorded in
CCT 1, 4. He also occurs as a creditor in the unpublished letter Kayseri 1746, probably at
a time when he was already dead. According to this letter, Enlil-bâni receives a message
from his representatives in Kanish to the effect that the colony wants to repay its debts
(5-6: ana kaspim sa habbulicni izakkûma). The contents of this letter and the way the
colony settled its debts will be discussed later in 11.11.
It is evident that the information provided by the texts concerning Enlil-bâni as a
creditor offers only a very limited insight into the way the Kanish colony obtained funds
by means of borrowing silver. Nevertheless, these references may be representative of the
way such transactions took place and were recorded in writing. Several letters contain a

During the nikkassü sa karim, 'the accounting of the karum', often called simply the
nikkassü, the balances were drawn up, and if a merchant had not deposited the full amOunt
of the datum fixed for him, he had to make a balance payment (nipiltum). Text kt c/k 1500
recordS three financial transactiOns conducted by or on behalf of Asgur-emiigi son Of
BuzutAya with two different karü. They provide chrOnological details frOm which the date of
each accounting can be derived. The first is an acknowledgment by the karum of
Purushattum that Assur-emugf paid them an amOunt of copper as a balance payment for
another merchant, which is dated to month V of the eponym year of Assur-imittf; the secOnd
and third involve payments On behalf of Aggur-emugi to the karum of Kanish connected
with the accounting, and both are dated to mOnth XI Of the eponym year of Ennamânum.
The fourth records a debt that could have Originated from a bal ance payment, dated to month
V Of the eponym year of Aggur-mâlik. 551 In the letter kt a/k 474, Adad-sulülf is told that
during the accounting in the karum-office it was established that he had to make a balance
payment to anOther person. As this payment is expressed in copper, it is possible that the
location of the accounting was Purushattum. It is difficult to determine how far all these
payments were connected with sitapkum. There are thus at least two months in which the
nikkassü sa karim was held, month V attested fOr Purushattum(?), and month XI for
Kanish. It is possible that an accounting toOk place in both towns during bOths months, sO
that every half year the accounts were prepared. Alternatively, each tOwn, including those
not mentioned in the twO texts, cOuld have held its accOunting once a year in a particular
month. Several references in other texts demonstrate that the accounting took place
periOdically ('the next n.' , CCT 2, 6.41; 'there will be a n. in fOur mOnths', BIN 4, 28.24),
and the passage 'I assumed liability for the accounting instead of our father in the year when

The names Hamala, Iarsumelka, Sulmu-sa-Assur, Usher, Dakü and Wadii occur here
for the first time in a Kültepe text. The name IIarsumalka (a variant of Harsumelka) is
known from an iggàti-text from Ali pr (OIP 27, 49 A:1, B:6). Six persons in that text are
said to be from the city Amkuwa. Because the name is so rare and since lines 14-15 state
that `He will bring Harsumelka', it seems that Harsumelka was living in a different city,
perhaps in Amkuwa. If that is true, these two persons may have been the same.
The topics in the text on the tablet are as follows:
1-6)
The names of the persons that started the case.
6-8)
Declaration made by the witnesses that these persons started the case of their free
will.
8-13) The special decision of the king of Kanis to give the large house of Salim-Assur
to Hamala.
14-18) Salim-Assur's daughter Harsumelka, who is the wife of Hamala, must be brought
into the house and the priestess Ziki is going to live with them.
18-30) If Hamala and his wife maltreat Ziki she will get everything that she received
from her father as her share; she may leave the house and can stay with her
brothers.
30-36) The brothers are free to go where they want, they do not have to obey to the
arhàlum. They will receive a small house outside the city.
36-43) The brothers have to support Ziki.
43-50) After Ziki's death Hamala must give the documents of Salim-Assur to the
brothers.
51-54) Hamala is not responsible for Salim-Assur's debts.

Appendix: the evidence
The evidence for arhâlum and unussum as well as a selection of the evidence for the
terms tuzinnum and ubadinnum can be found in transliteration and translation below. The
texts have, where possible, been grouped chronologically as those from Level II and
those from the subsequent Level Ib. The so-called notarization clause, stating that the
transaction was done under the jurisdiction of (iggâté) the king and the Chief of the
Staircase, is typical for Anatolian deeds from Level Ib; it even occurs in debt-notes from
that period. The absence of this clause in kt 87/k 39 — as in kt k/k 35a (Bayram &
Veenhof 1993: 99), where the same Kalua rabi mahirim occurs —, in Münster 2432 and
Kay 294, as well as in SUP 1, dates those texts in Level II. Several of the texts first
published by V. Donbaz are here given in a different reading and translation; these
differences have not been indicated.

whether the seal on the lower edge of the Münster fragment is that of Zabarasna. Nothing is
known about Kurduba or the circumstances of the debt that caused him to be sold.

C. GÜNBATTI
The findspot and the general condition of the treaty texts
The Excavation Director Prof. Dr. Tahsin Özgüç informed me that the two tablets
were unearthed in the Karum at plansquare L/114, adjacent to XLIX/115, in which 230
tablets were discovered in 2001, 140 of which were from Level Ib. He also stated that the
rooms had no specific architectural or archaeological features.
Unfortunately these two tablets were not preserved in good condition. Kt. 00/k 6 was
broken into two and stuck. The tablet consists of 90 lines. Especially the obverse is in
terrible condition and is difficult to identify a meaningful sentence. The reverse is in
better condition. The left edge with 6 lines of text is also broken and most of it is missing.
The tablet contains the text of a treaty between Assur and Kanis. The subjects of both
parties are called mer Assur 'a citizen of Assur' and mer Kànis 'a citizen of Kanis'.
Kt. 00/k 10 has four columns and with this feature it is unique at Kültepe. Almost half
of the tablet is missing. Collected and adhered pieces are also in bad condition,
consequently there is no single line with all the signs preserved. I assume that the tablet
consisted of 250 lines, however only 124 lines were preserved including some lines with
only a few remaining signs. The expressions mer Assur 'a citizen of Assur' and mer
Hahhim 'a citizen of Hahhum' or mer kârim Hahhim 'one from the Hahhum colony'
make it clear that the treaty was concluded between Hahhum and Assur.
I shall first present Kt. 00/k 6, the treaty with Kanis, and then Kt. 00/k 10, the treaty
with Hahhum.8

Appendix: the evidence
The evidence for arhâlum and unussum as well as a selection of the evidence for the
terms tuzinnum and ubadinnum can be found in transliteration and translation below. The
texts have, where possible, been grouped chronologically as those from Level II and
those from the subsequent Level Ib. The so-called notarization clause, stating that the
transaction was done under the jurisdiction of (iggâté) the king and the Chief of the
Staircase, is typical for Anatolian deeds from Level Ib; it even occurs in debt-notes from
that period. The absence of this clause in kt 87/k 39 — as in kt k/k 35a (Bayram &
Veenhof 1993: 99), where the same Kalua rabi mahirim occurs —, in Münster 2432 and
Kay 294, as well as in SUP 1, dates those texts in Level II. Several of the texts first
published by V. Donbaz are here given in a different reading and translation; these
differences have not been indicated.

5'-11' If <anybody> from the ubadinnum, be it Zabarasna or his servants raises a claim for
Kurduba they will pay 5 minas of silver to him.
Note:
9': Kienast read Ur-du-ba. The last sign is a clear su on the copy by Schaudig.
The name Zabarasna occurs in several other Old Assyrian texts where it may well refer to the
same person. The fact that he possesses a domain with dependants identifies him as an important
inhabitant of ancient Kanis. Zabarasna married a woman named Kulzia according to KTS 2, 6 (=
AKT 1, 21; when the couple dies, the house falls to HiKtahsusar and Peruwa). He is a witness and
seals in TC 2, 66 (envelope; tablet is TC 3, 240); he îs also a witness in VS 26, 101 (see below).
Since the seal impression in TC 2, 66 does not appear to have been published, it remains unclear
whether the seal on the lower edge of the Münster fragment is that of Zabarasna. Nothing is
known about Kurduba or the circumstances of the debt that caused him to be sold.

C. GÜNBATTI
The findspot and the general condition of the treaty texts
The Excavation Director Prof. Dr. Tahsin Özgüç informed me that the two tablets
were unearthed in the Karum at plansquare L/114, adjacent to XLIX/115, in which 230
tablets were discovered in 2001, 140 of which were from Level Ib. He also stated that the
rooms had no specific architectural or archaeological features.
Unfortunately these two tablets were not preserved in good condition. Kt. 00/k 6 was
broken into two and stuck. The tablet consists of 90 lines. Especially the obverse is in
terrible condition and is difficult to identify a meaningful sentence. The reverse is in
better condition. The left edge with 6 lines of text is also broken and most of it is missing.
The tablet contains the text of a treaty between Assur and Kanis. The subjects of both
parties are called mer Assur 'a citizen of Assur' and mer Kànis 'a citizen of Kanis'.
Kt. 00/k 10 has four columns and with this feature it is unique at Kültepe. Almost half
of the tablet is missing. Collected and adhered pieces are also in bad condition,
consequently there is no single line with all the signs preserved. I assume that the tablet
consisted of 250 lines, however only 124 lines were preserved including some lines with
only a few remaining signs. The expressions mer Assur 'a citizen of Assur' and mer
Hahhim 'a citizen of Hahhum' or mer kârim Hahhim 'one from the Hahhum colony'
make it clear that the treaty was concluded between Hahhum and Assur.
I shall first present Kt. 00/k 6, the treaty with Kanis, and then Kt. 00/k 10, the treaty
with Hahhum.8

2. THE MERCHANTS
There was a social distinction in Assur as well as in the Assyrian communities abroad
between ‘big’ (rabium) and ‘small’ (ṣahhurum) free citizens (awīlum). It was defined
along family lines, as a remark by the daughter and sons of the deceased Pūšu-kēn
makes clear when they write in BIN 6, 59: “And since (Kulumāya) left he has shown
contempt towards our father’s spirit and [even] us he has thereby [treated] as ‘small’
persons”.17 Attaining a good position could be the responsibility of an adoptive father.18
Families and individuals from both layers of society were actively involved in trade,
with the merchants belonging to the ‘big’ people, the citizens holding slaves. Others
besides professional merchants bought and sold to make some extra money. In the
first place there were the female relatives of the traders, who manufactured textiles
at home and sold these via their men in Anatolia. The king of Assur also entrusted
merchandise to a trusted merchant, but it is not known how often the kings did this.
According to KTS 1, 30, Asqūdum (perhaps the same individual as the ‘palace servant’
by that name mentioned in KTS 1, 55b) had received two donkeys loaded with 125
minas of tin, 30 kutānus, over 5 minas of extra-fine lapis lazuli and a lump of amutum-
iron weighing 11 shekels to convey to Anatolia. Aduda, son of king Šarru-kēn, was
active in Kanesh.19 A senior official in the administration of the city-state, the lapputāum

higher price there influenced asking prices in Anatolia according to Pa. 22 (L29–579):
“Thus says Imdilum, speak to Aššur-ṭāb: Adu is bringing 2 talents 2 minas of tin and
5 good quality kutānus to you under my seals. (...). 6 shekels each for my tin and 15
shekels each for my textiles, sell (the textiles) together with the tin for cash. If that
cannot be done, let my tin remain packed (lit.: under its sealings). I repeatedly informed
you that tin is delayed. Although I informed you (about this), you write to me in your
letter: ‘I have sold your tin at 7 shekels each.’ Report to me if there is still unsold tin
left. I must not get angry. But if you have already sold (it), send me the refined silver
– the silver of the qīptum – under seal. And (sell) my textiles at 15 shekels each!”
We know of one particular case in which the city of Assur responded to a temporary
shortage of tin, its main import. According to a decision by the city assembly, “one
can (only) buy tin for one-third (of the money)”.49 The motivation for this decision to
limit expenditure was clearly to distribute more evenly among the merchants later
on the extra tin that would reach the market once the expected caravan from the
Lower Country arrived.

7. GOLD
Gold has a special position among the objects of trade.77 It was a highly prized material
and one letter contains the somewhat deprecatory remark “When they see gold, (their)
hands and feet tremble” referring to unspecified “men” (awīlū).78 It was made into
jewellery and formed the valuta of the naruqqum-joint-stock investments in a way that
is still imperfectly understood. But most importantly, gold was most fitting as an
offering for the gods. The commonest reference to votive offerings (ikribum) concerns
golden sun-symbols (šamšum).79 The strong value attached to gold by the city of Assur
is apparent in the law that prohibited the sale of gold to non-Assyrians which is alluded
to in an official letter:
“Thus (said) the ruler, speak to the Kanesh colony: The tablet containing the
verdict of the City concerning gold which we sent to you, that tablet has been
cancelled. We did not draw up any (new) rule about gold. The rule concerning
gold is the same as previously: one may sell it to another, (but) in accordance
with the wording on the stele: no Assyrian whatever shall give gold to an
Akkadian, an Amorite, or a Shubarean. Whoever does so shall not remain
alive.”80
This policy can be explained from the motive of trade: the city needed the gold to pay
for the imported tin and as part of the financing of naruqqus. Hoarding could also have
been a motive, and the obvious benefactors in the OA context would be the temples

which was sent to Anatolia to be sold there as a tadmiqtum. Such a dire situation is
vividly described in some of the letters sent by Tāram-Kūbi to her husband Innāya. A
letter from Assur sent to Alahum contains the following lines: “You wrote to me: ‘Send
me 2 kutānus!’ I fell ill and spent the 10 shekels of silver that you had sent me. I had
to stay in bed for 2 months, but (your) representatives did not ask how I was doing.
Nor did they give me an offering for expenses. Ever since you left (Assur) they never
gave me a single shekel of silver (...). If you are my father, let your message come here
and just as the (men of) the town give a subsistence allowance to their daughters, so
may they give me (one).”110
A moving letter is AKT 4, 63, possibly written by a gubabtum-priestess: “Do those
who become angry with their sisters remain angry for ever? What have I done to you?
Ever since you departed ten years ago, you do not mention my name. I am living in
my own house and you are troubling yourself. You are my brother! Help me with a
shekel of silver and I will pray on your behalf in front of my god Aššur.”111
A rare example of a man writing about similar shortages from a town somewhere
in Anatolia is contained in CCT 4, 45b: “My dear brother, send me there 15 or 20 minas
of wool so that I can leave (that) behind with them (fem.) (to pay for) their (fem.)
food. Then I will get ready and depart. Why have you locked me in the city like a
woman for ten months? And here nobody gives me a loan. Here, winter just caught
up with me. There is not even a single loaf of bread or firewood or textiles to clothe
them (fem.).”112
Providing the necessities of life was the responsibility of the husband or father and
those unwilling to comply could be forced to do so by court order. This appears from
a verdict by the colony at Wahšušana (Kt 88/k 269, Bayram and Çeçen 1995, 11),
according to which an Assyrian merchant, who had left his wife behind without any
means of subsistence, had to provide her with a monthly allowance of 8 minas of
tim (15) i-mu-a-at-ma lá ta-ša-ra-[ni (x)], “The silver that comes here has been paid for the house of
Pilah-Ištar. Even the share of Aššur-nādā has been paid to the City Hall for his debt. There is here
not a single shekel of silver for us to live on. The children are dying from hunger and you do not
take care of me.”

Text 12- Prague I 478. A scribe instructs a man on his guarantor-duty.495
Gestellungsbiirgschaft,496 which was to ensure that another legal party appears for a legal

stake, which would become the burden of the guarantor if he neglected his duty. As in the

authorities. The detailed dialogue in this text raises the question as to what extent private
parties engaged scribes at a daily basis in purely oral procedures. Obviously, we cannot
answer this, but no doubt scribes would have been much more active than the textual

argument pursued by the attorney. According to the factual witnesses, Sueyya had
apparently come to Ennam-Assur's house with two separate bags containing 40 minas of
silver in all. But Ennam-Assur had complained that the bags needed to be stored in a
container rather than lying around in his house separately. The relevance of this piece of
information in not clear and Ennam-Assur may simply have been a man who kept a tidy
house. But his request may also indicate that he actually knew the silver belonged to
Sueyya, and accordingly that he didn't want to confuse his own funds stored in his house
with those belonging to another man.
Additional ambiguity with respect to the ownership of the silver arises from the
statement that the container eventually was "brought in(to Ennam-Assur's house)"
(serubum), which in technical legal terms could mean that the silver had been delivered
as a pledge by Sueyya. On the other hand, the factual witnesses also stated that "they"
brought in the container, where "they" refer to Sueyya and his unnamed fellows. This
emphasis would hardly make sense had the transaction in question been concerned with a
pledge extended personally from Sueyya to Ennam-Assur. Instead, it indicates that the
expression "to bring X in(to PN's house)" had a literal rather than a technical meaning in
this case. 1136

be taken.

Kywwexä
Iddin-Istar writes to his father Aššur-nàdà about his activities for the funs in Durhumit. He was
apparently in part responsible for the firm's trade in copper, and this letter shows us the basic
procedures involved. Iddin-Istar collected debts to the firm and had brought a amount of tin as
well; in Durhumit he could collect raw copper of low quality, and this then had to be brought to
other places in Anatolia—in this case Burushaddum—where it could be exchanged for copper of
good quality. This would then have to be sold again for silver. In this particular letter Iddin-Istar
appears to be entirely dependent on his father's orders and advice, and he may not have been very
experienced at the time. Ili-àlum, his uncle, therefore had no luck in persuading him to let him take
care of the deal.

The text is too fragmentary for a translation but it gives some hints: five or more seal
owners, all joined in an enterprise, do a kind of partnership in mutual agreement (line 9: i-
na mi-ig-ra-ti-su-nu). The city of Wahgusana is mentioned together with the City (alum)
and the prince (rub 'um), that may mean that the parties have sworn an oath by the city
and the prince (lines 10, 12). The text mentions again Eddin-Agsur and his father Ahiaya
(1. 4) and the other intervening people with their father's name e.g. X-x-ba-ni son of I-di-
a-[x] can be reconstructed as Aggur-bâni, attested in the wrongly glued small fragment at
the bottom of the obverse; Inbi-Igtar, son of Assur-mugallim (I. 2), X-Bélum (probably to
be read Sû-Bélum), son of Imdi-Igtar (1. 3), and the important trader Aggur-mâlik
mentioned 5 times here (I. 6.3'.2'.15' and at the edge of the obverse). He seems to be the
central person of this document; whether he is a son of Aggur-bâni, as we have proposed,
cannot be proven on the basis of this tablet. On one side of the wrongly glued reverse we
read: "he will assume the responsibility i-za-az (I') and they will not claim anything
from Aggur-malik and his son" (2'-4'). Towards the end of the reverse it says that
somebody will not claim anything against Assur-malik (14'-16'). On the correctly
positioned reverse the text states that they have seized Assur-malik for a conflict (Aggur-
malik DUMU ... is-bu-tù-su). Two incomplete names occuring in Kt n/k 28 and Kt n/k
29 as Su-a-[...] (Kt n/k 28,17; Kt n/k 29,I') and [...]-Szr-en6 (Kt n/k 28,3; Kt n/k 29,7.5')
could not be deciphered with certainty; the fact that the latter is referred to as being a son
of A[dad-bâni] in Kt n/k 28,3 needs further proof.

2. Brief des Puzur-Assur
Geschäftsbrief des Puzur-Asgur an Püsu-kén: Puzur-Assur beklagt sich beredt
darüber, dass Püsu-kén Verleumdungen Gehör schenkt und damit die bisherigen guten
Geschäftsbeziehungen aufs Spiel setzt. Zumal auch Gerüchte über aussereheliche Be-
ziehungen zu einem namentlich nicht genannten Mädchen angesprochen werden (Z. 19-
24), ist der Brief sehr emotional gehalten, mit Folgen für die Syntax. Puzur-Assur gibt zu
sich verspekuliert zu haben und bittet um Geduld. Puzur-Assur hat offenbar seine
Investitutionen eigenmächtig reduziert (vgl. Z. 28-30.), was Pâgu-ken zu verschiedenen
Vorsichtsmassnahmen veranlasst hat (Z. 2b-18). Unvermittelt wird Puzur-Aggur dann
wieder ganz geschäftsmässig, indem er verschiedene Anweisungen erteilt (Z. 31-39).

V. DONBAZ
The text is too fragmentary for a translation but it gives some hints: five or more seal
owners, all joined in an enterprise, do a kind of partnership in mutual agreement (line 9: i-
na mi-ig-ra-ti-su-nu). The city of Wahgusana is mentioned together with the City (alum)
and the prince (rub 'um), that may mean that the parties have sworn an oath by the city
and the prince (lines 10, 12). The text mentions again Eddin-Agsur and his father Ahiaya
(1. 4) and the other intervening people with their father's name e.g. X-x-ba-ni son of I-di-
a-[x] can be reconstructed as Aggur-bâni, attested in the wrongly glued small fragment at
the bottom of the obverse; Inbi-Igtar, son of Assur-mugallim (I. 2), X-Bélum (probably to
be read Sû-Bélum), son of Imdi-Igtar (1. 3), and the important trader Aggur-mâlik
mentioned 5 times here (I. 6.3'.2'.15' and at the edge of the obverse). He seems to be the
central person of this document; whether he is a son of Aggur-bâni, as we have proposed,
cannot be proven on the basis of this tablet. On one side of the wrongly glued reverse we
read: "he will assume the responsibility i-za-az (I') and they will not claim anything
from Aggur-malik and his son" (2'-4'). Towards the end of the reverse it says that
somebody will not claim anything against Assur-malik (14'-16'). On the correctly
positioned reverse the text states that they have seized Assur-malik for a conflict (Aggur-
malik DUMU ... is-bu-tù-su). Two incomplete names occuring in Kt n/k 28 and Kt n/k
29 as Su-a-[...] (Kt n/k 28,17; Kt n/k 29,I') and [...]-Szr-en6 (Kt n/k 28,3; Kt n/k 29,7.5')
could not be deciphered with certainty; the fact that the latter is referred to as being a son
of A[dad-bâni] in Kt n/k 28,3 needs further proof.

beginning of each line there is a ve rtical wedge and there are four more vertical wedges
scattered in the text, before some personal names (I. 5, 15, 41, 55). The list contains the
names of 104 eponyms and starts at the beginning of the reign of Irigum I. The name of
each eponym is followed, with a few exceptions, by the father's name.

1-2. To Aššur-emuqi;
from Dadiya:
3-16. Laqepum, son of Akazi, owes me 3 minas of silver; I hold his certified tablet. He holds my
working capital. Moreover, I have given him 7 minas of tin for purchases. Thereof he has returned
3 minas minus l shekel of tin to me; 4 minas l shekel is still in his possession. Then he took 'A
mina of silver from my outstanding credits-so I have many accountings with him!
17-22. He treats me like an evil man and hides himself from me. Indeed, he keeps following roads of his
own wish!
23-35. As you are my brother, seize whatever he has in his possession there, be it silver or goods! Also,
where goods belonging to him may be found with strangers, seize (them)! Act decisively! And
then bring him here personally. If he objects, then take him before the harbor (authorities). In my
presence they will examine the excesses he has committed!

This interesting text, unfortunately not entirely understood, deals with a problem that must have worried
many Old Assyrian traders: moths destroying their valuable woolen textiles. The subject is also referred to
briefly in G. Contenau, TTC, no. 14.

There was a range of terms used to described the peregrinations of the merchants, and Veenhof’s review
makes its most important contributions by approaching the trade through the terminology, aiming to describe
methodologically the communication through the constellation of vocabulary. The limitations of the evidence for
providing precise definitions of terms referring to travelers—specifically ālikum, was̄ium,and bātiqum—and to the
terms ḫarrānum and ellutum are well known. Nonetheless, the following general constellation of relationships
might be suggested. The term ālikum must refer generally to a traveler. If a more specific meaning is sought, then
it may refer to peregrinating merchants. To “join a traveler” (išti ālikim ṭaḫḫu’um) meant to join a small group of
peregrinators and accompanying occasional travelers as they left the city. Likewise, wāṣium had a general
connotation. Either an ālikum or wāṣium could be travelling in a larger group, not necessarily alone. By contrast,
the term bātiqum finds its most important distinction as ‘detached traveler.’ In a context which did not necessitate
the distinction, the same bātiqum traveler could have been referred to by the term ālikum. In regards to speed, it
seems prudent to propose that an ālikum or bātiqum could be fast or slow depending on the individual needs of
that person or group. While the bātiqum has been taken to represent a faster mode of travel, the
interchangeability of attested formulas—“Send your message with the first ālikum/wāṣium/bātiqum”—seems to
reflect the preference of the correspondent rather than materially different phenomena.

56 Translation of the last clause is conjecture. I translate aṣṣer ištu 5 warḫī i-Kuriya atanalluku (subjunctive
verb following aṣṣer) to reflect the similarity to the use of aṣṣer plus a nominal phrase, which is often meant to
convey “In addition to …”. i-Ku-ri-ya could alternatively be read i-ma-ri-a, to construe an interpretation in which
Pūšu-kēn had been running from(?) his son for five months. This reading is strained and unlikely. A spelling
reflecting the open syllable in mer’a would be expected (i.e. i-ma-ar-i-a), though forms parallel to this one do exist
(ATHE 21a:10 ma-ru, see GKT §28d). On the other hand, reading i-ku-ri-a (suggested by Lewy KVA) does not yield a
clearly plausible answer. A personal name I-ku-ri (kt 94/k 288:3, 16, 17) leaves I-ku-ri-a as a related hypochoristic
(or Pūšu-kēn refering to Ikuri as “my Ikuri”) without a clear grammatical role in the clause. Reading i-Ku-ri-a
yields a reasonable personal name (Kuriya: see OIP 27 55:37, kt 87/k 404:8, 89/k 257:9, kt a/k 624:3). Another
possibility could be i-Ku-<za>-ri-«a» (where za! was transposed with ri) who is mentioned in 5.11:4, 16.

1-2Šū-Ḫubur to Pūšu-kēn:
3-15(Concerning) the house next to yours which the estate of Ilī-mālik sold, we said, “We
will move the qablītum.” As for me, I went to this place but he would not sell the house.
Afterwards, I gave instructions to your representatives and my representatives that they
should buy the house for you. If your representatives and my representatives have not
purchased the house before my arrival, within a year, I will buy it for you at my arrival. I will
not leave it to them.
16-26Concerning the talent of tin which Aššur-mālik and Irma-Aššur entrusted to Lalum
in Ḫaḫḫum, here, I seized the house of Lalum on account of this tin, and they said, “Arraign
your witnesses.” Urgent! There let Aššur-mālik and Irma-Aššur document their testimonies
concerning when they gave Lalum the tin so that the oaths may seize the roughly 10 minas
silver of my outstanding claims. Seal and send the silver to me.
31-36If Lalum’s representatives are there, may the men clear them of their obligations so
that they give me the silver so that I can accordingly give it to Hawilia.

70 šibīšunu ša inūmi ammakam ana Lalim iddinūni ludanninū-ma -- elsewhere translated “making witnesses
strong,” see T. Hertel, "Old Assyrian Legal Practices: An Anthropological Perspective on Legal Disputes in the
Ancient Near East" (Ph.D. Dissertation, University of Copenhagen, 2007), 110 n. 301. This phrase referred to a
procedure of stating testimony before the divine image, often the dagger of Aššur. The testimonies were recorded
on tablets.

nos. 5, 8 and 20. The sale contract exhibits what Kienast (op. cit., ª 60) calls the “bilateral formulary

notes back and cancelled them by breaking their cases, but for some reason (to keep an overview of

E. ROBSON
BUILDING WITH BRICKS AND MORTAR
183
building materials, digging canals and building different sorts of walls, as well as
rates of pay2. There is also a sophisticated system for counting standardised bricks
and estimating how many will be needed [Powell 1982: especially 119]. Although
around a dozen different sizes of bricks are mentioned in OB maths, the commonest
are the 2/3-cubit square baked brick, SIG4 / libittum (Type 8 in Powell's typology),
and the smaller rectangular unbaked brick, 15 by 10 fingers long, SIG4.AL.ÙR.RA /
agurrum (Type 2). Both are 5 fingers thick 3 .
Bricks are counted in groups of 720, the brick-sar. The nalbanum, an important
concept in Old Babylonian mathematics, is defined as the number of brick-sar in a
volume-sar. Because each size of bricks has a specific nalbanum the number of
bricks needed for a wall can easily be estimated. Multiplying the volume of that wall,
in volume-sar, by the nalbanum of the bricks to be used gives the number of bricks
needed, counted in brick-sar:
bricks = length x width x height x nalbanum.
This method assumes that the wall is composed entirely of bricks, but there is usually
mortar too, and perhaps a waterproofing course of bitumen. Any estimate made
using the method described will give too high a number of bricks. None the less, it is
this method that is found in all the OB maths texts so far published 4 .
However, an Old Babylonian fragment from the British Museum, BM 96957, shows
that more sophisticated methods were known. Christopher Walker kindly drew my
attention to this tablet. He did much of the preliminary work on it and has provided
the hand copy published here. It joins VAT 6598 [Neugebauer 1935-7: I 277-287, II
pl. 17, 44, III 57], and it is now clear that the two pieces were part of a three column
tablet, although there is still a substantial piece missing. The top of the single
remaining column on the obverse of the VAT 6598 joins the bottom of the third
column of BM 96957. The subject of the reverse is rectangles and the lengths of their
diagonals, but the ten extant problems on the obverse and the first problem on the
reverse (VAT 6598) show how to estimate the number of bricks in a wall and in a
house. For reasons of space and subject matter only the obverse is discussed here.

I 1-4. A wall. The width is 2 cubits, the length 2 1/2 nindan, the height 1 1/2 nindan5 .
How many bricks? You: multiply 2 cubits, the width, by 2 1/2 nindan, the length.
You will see 0;25 (the area). Multiply 0;25 by 18, the height. You will see 7;30 (7 1/2
sar, the volume). Multiply 7;30 by 6, the coefficient of a wall. You will see 45. The
bricks are 45 sar. The method.
15 -10. A wall. The length is 2 1/2 nindan, the height 1 1/2 nindan, the bricks 45
sar. What is the width of my wall? You: multiply 2;30, the length, by 18, the height,
and you will see 45. Keep., Take the reciprocal (the reciprocal) of 6, the cOefficient
of a wall; multiply by 45 sar, the bricks. You will see 7;30 (the volume). Keep. Take
the reciprocal of 45 that you are keeping. You will see 0;01 20. Multiply 0;01 20 by
7;30 (the volume) that you are keeping and you will see 0;10. The width of the wall
is 2 cubits. The method.
II 1 -4. [A wall. The height is 1 1/2 nindan, the bricks 45 sar. The length exceeds
the width of the wall by 2;20 nindan. What are the length and width of my wall?
You: take the reciprocal of 6, the coefficient of a wall. You will see 0;10. Multiply
0;10 by 45 sar, the bricks. You will see 7;30. 7 1/2 sar is the volume. Take the
reciprocal of 18, the height. You will see 0;03 20. Multiply 0;03 20 by 7;30. You
will see 0;25. The area is 0;25. Keep. Break in half 2;20, by which the length exceeds
the width of the wall. You will see 1;10. Put down 1;10 twice. Square.] You will see
1;21 40. Add 0;25 that you are keeping to 1;21 40. You will see 1;46 40. What is the
square root of 1;46 40? 1;20 is the square root. Put down twice. Add 1;10 to 1;20.
You will see 2;30. The length of the wall is 2;30. Take 1;10 from 1;20. The
remainder is 0;10. The width of the wall is 2 cubits. The method.
II 5-8. The <area of the> house is 5 sar. For a height of 2 1/2 nindan how many
bricks should I get made? You: take a third of 5 sar. You will see 1;40 (the walls).
Multiply 1;40 by 2 1/2 nindan, the height. You will see 4;10. You will get 2 1/2 iku
bricks made and you will pile up 5 sar house to a height of 2 1/2 nindan. The method.
II 9-13. If the bricks are 2 1/2 iku, the height 2 1/2 nindan, how much house
should I build? You: take the reciprocal of 2 1/2 nindan, the height. Multiply by 4;10,
the 2 1/2 iku bricks. You will see 1;40. Keep. Take the reciprocal of 0;20, the
coefficient of a built house. You will see 3. Multiply 3 by 1;40 that you are keeping.
You will see 5. The <area of the> house is 5 sar. The method.
